Subject: Peaking behavior / commit sizing question

Hey Jonas —

Quick context: Summit AI is building a customer-facing assistant that does multi-turn summarization + retrieval-augmented generation. We expect fairly spiky traffic: short steady-state baseline (~300 TPS of small prompts) with planned marketing-driven peaks where bursts hit ~2.5k concurrent requests for ~10–30 minutes.

We need help mapping a committed dedicated pool to realistic tokens/sec and p95 latency SLOs. Specifically:
- How do you translate our peak request mix into tokens/sec and GPU count?
- How much reserve should we commit to cover 99th/99.9th tail during these marketing spikes without blasting our unit economics?
- Any recommended fallback or multi-variant strategy to keep user-facing p95 under 600ms?

Attached a high-level example of our request size distribution (avg tokens/in = 120, avg tokens/out = 200) and target SLOs.

Thanks —
Arjun
Head of Infrastructure, Summit AI

Arjun —

Thanks for the context and the profile — this is exactly the sort of detail we need. Quick, high-level read: with avg in/out tokens you sent and a spike concurrency of ~2.5k, there are two common sizing levers we use to map to dedicated GPU pools: tokens/sec (aggregate token throughput) and tail latency cushion (headroom %).

Initial assumptions I made for a back-of-envelope (we'll validate with engineering below):
- Model class: Mistral-XXL style (2.5–3B equivalent inference characteristics) — you said retrieval + RAG so expect ~80–120 tokens/sec per A100 equiv for this mix when using our typical quantized runtime and warmed KV cache.
- Average prompt roundtrip (120 in / 200 out) -> ~320 tokens per request. At 2.5k concurrent requests that's ~800k tokens active (concurrent * avg tokens), but throughput depends on concurrency arrival pattern.

I'll loop in Kim and Prio to convert this to a recommended committed slab, burst strategy, and a visible p95/P99 projection. Expect a more detailed note in 24–36h.

Also included: quick checklist of questions that will materially change the sizing:
- confirmation of model family (if you're running a larger decoder the per-GPU tokens/sec reduces)
- tolerance for quantization (we can propose q4 variants)
- percent of requests that hit retrieval vs generation-only (retrieval increases latency but may reduce token generation in some flows)

Cheers,
Jonas Weber
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: kimberly_park@redwood.com

Subject: RE: Summit AI - peaking latency tail & reserve sizing discussion

Looping in our capacity math team — I pulled the spreadsheet and ran a couple of quick sims. Key points up-front:

- Baseline mapping: using the request shape and assuming Mistral-class model at q4_0, a single H100-equivalent slot can sustain ~150–220 tokens/sec for your average mixed workload when KV cache hit rate is high.
- Burst delta: short marketing spikes where arrival rate jumps produce higher concurrent KV warmups — those can drop effective tokens/sec per device by ~20–35% for the first 30–120s unless we pre-warm cache.

Preliminary sizing (conservative):
- Sustained baseline (300 TPS, 320 tokens/request): ~96k tokens/sec -> 440–640 tokens/sec per H100 implies 150–220 H100-equivalents (this is baseline spread across many requests; we should consider lower-cost smaller-gpu shapes for baseline if latency tolerance is higher).
- Peak target (2.5k concurrent bursts with 30s median duration): instantaneous token pressure ~800k tokens active; mapped to throughput you'll need a committed pool providing ~2.5k–3.5k tokens/sec headroom above baseline to reduce p95 risk. In practice that's an additional ~15–25 H100-equivalent reserved slots for burst smoothing if using our automatic short-term burst allocation.

Recommendations before Priyom provides final numbers:
1) Commit to a baseline slab sized for 1.5x steady-state (covers growth + modest burst tails).
2) Purchase a small burst credit pack (monthly) to cover the 10–30 minute marketing spikes rather than over-committing GPUs at list price.
3) Enable prefix-caching and proactive KV-warm on rollout windows we expect spikes.

Assigning Priyom to produce a tokens/sec -> GPU-equivalent table with p95/p99 projections and two commit scenarios (conservative vs cost-lean).

- Kim

Attaching a compact table in-line below (quick read) — I validated against our per-VM A/B kernels using the telemetry from the last Mistral-class onboarding. Assumptions: q4_0 quantized runtime, KV cache hit rate 85% after warm, average seq_len_in=120 seq_len_out=200, arrival distribution Gumbel-like with 30s burst mode for marketing traffic.

Summary conversions (rounded):
- Effective tokens/sec per H100-equivalent (steady): 200 tps
- Effective tokens/sec per H100-equivalent (cold-warm transient first 60s): 135 tps
- p95 single-request latency target mapping: to keep user-facing p95 < 600ms we need per-request processing parallelism and average device utilization < 72% (higher utilization multiplies tail).

Table (values as guidance):
- Baseline token throughput requirement: 96,000 tokens/sec (300 req/s * 320 tokens)
- Required committed H100-equivalents for baseline (steady): 480 H100-equiv (96,000 / 200)
- Conservative committed slab (1.5x baseline): 720 H100-equiv (provides growth cushion + 1.5x load)
- Burst cushion required to absorb 2.5k concurrent marketing spike w/o violating p95: additional 40–60 H100-equiv transiently (these can be satisfied via burst credits or short-term autoscale if Dedicated allows burst leases)

Headroom policy suggestion: commit to conservative slab (720 equiv) but configure two policies:
1) Canary-scaled pre-warm: at T-5m to an expected event, pre-warm an extra 30 H100-equiv to raise cache hit rates.
2) On-demand short burst credit (monthly package covering ~2–3 hours of burst at 50–60 extra equiv) vs over-commit at list price.

Cost guidance (very rough): dedicated monthly unit pricing + burst credits should be modeled; will add concrete numbers after we pick exact VM type(s) (A100 vs H100 equivalents differ ~10–25% on sustained throughput per device depending on kernel).

Risks / tradeoffs:
- Over-commit increases fixed cost but reduces risk and improves p95 predictability.
- Reliance on burst credits reduces fixed cost but risks short-term throttling if bursts exceed purchased credits or if regional capacity constrained.

I'll produce a short spreadsheet with per-GPU numbers and a p95/p99 projection by EOD tomorrow.

—Priyom

Arjun —

Thanks for the patience. Summarizing our recommended starting plan so your procurement and infra teams can review:

1) Baseline commit: 720 H100-equivalents (covers 1.5x steady-state per our conservative scenario). This maps to ~96k tokens/sec baseline with per-device effective 200 tps headroom.
2) Burst strategy: purchase the monthly burst credit pack that provides the equivalent of 50 H100-equiv for short windows (covers typical 10–30m campaign spikes without over-committing).
3) Pre-warm policy: set an event-driven pre-warm to +30 H100-equiv at T-5m for scheduled campaigns to raise KV hit rate and reduce cold-warm losses.
4) Fallbacks & cost-containment: enable a graceful fallback pool that routes to a slightly quantized model variant (q4_0 -> q2_2 / smaller-context variant) when sustained auto-scale + burst credits are exhausted; configure routing to enforce p95 under 800ms for fallbacks.

Next steps:
- I'll send a Drive link with the per-GPU numbers and a sample SOW (attached). Please let me know if procurement needs a different cost bake (A100 vs H100).
- Can we schedule a 30m call Friday 3pm PT to walk the proposal with Summit infra & finance? If that works I'll create a calendar invite.

Thanks,
Jonas Weber
